activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked for orange paint. There was no orange. "Oh no," she said. "How can I paint my pumpkin orange?"

Her friend Milo sat next to her. Milo was painting with red paint. He had yellow paint too. He poured some red and some yellow into his cup. He stirred them with his brush. The paint turned orange! The paint smelled a little stinky, but Norah did not mind.

"Can I try that?" Norah asked. "Yes," said Milo. She put red in her cup. She put yellow in too. She stirred and stirred. Orange! She painted her pumpkin round and bright.

Teacher Ann came to look. "What a big orange pumpkin," she said. "Can I pay you with a sticker?" Norah grinned. "Yes, please." She stuck the sticker right on her smock.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We feel things by touching them with our skin, like our fingertips.
story:
Sofia wanted to play the senses game. Mama said, "Tell me each sense. Then find it in the house."

Sofia began with eyes. "I see with my eyes," she said. She looked out the window. She saw the moon, big and white.

"I hear with my ears." Then a dog barked outside. Sofia laughed. Her ears heard it fast.

"I smell with my nose." She sniffed the bread. "Mmm," she said.

"I taste with my tongue." Mama gave her a tiny taste of jam. It was sweet.

Then Sofia stopped. "What is the last one?" she asked. She felt a little worried she would forget.

Mama put a pine cone in her hand. Sofia touched it with her fingertips. "Ooh, it is bumpy," she said. She touched her soft blanket. Then her smooth cup.

"I feel with my fingers," she said. "My skin feels it all!"

Mama clapped. Sofia touched Mama's warm hand. "This feels the best," she said.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: One thing can belong to more than one group, like an apple is a food and also a fruit.
story:
Sarah ran into the library. "Books!" she said. "So many books!"

Today was story day. Miss Kim put out big cards. One card had a picture of animals. One had a picture of toys. One had a picture of foods.

"Put each card in its group," said Miss Kim.

Sarah picked up a cow. "Animals!" She put it down. Then she found a ball. "Toys!"

Then she held up an apple. "Foods!" she said.

Ben shook his head. "Fruits!" he said.

"You are both right," said Miss Kim. "Put it in two spots."

Sarah bent down. She set the apple with the foods. Then she picked it up again. She set it with the fruits too.

The apple sat in two places at once. Sarah laughed and clapped her hands.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: Each person uses their own toothbrush; people do not share toothbrushes.
story:
Aurora was three, and today was her first trip to the dentist. She sat in a big chair. It went up when the dentist pushed a button. A little wheel on the chair spun round and round. "Whee!" said Aurora.

The dentist had a surprise. "Pick a toothbrush," she said. "You get your very own." There was a pink one and a green one. Aurora took the pink one. But a young boy next to her grabbed it too. He held it tight.

"That is mine!" said Aurora. "Is it yours?" she asked him. "No," he said. "Mine is green. I took the wrong one." He put the pink one back. He took the green one instead. Now Aurora had pink, and he had green. "Two toothbrushes, two kids," said Aurora. "One for each!" The dentist laughed. "Let me see that smile," she said. Aurora opened her mouth wide, like a baby bird.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out.
story:
Athena ran into the backyard. Dad sat on the steps with his tea. "Stay where I can see you," he said. Athena chased a yellow butterfly. It flew past the big grill. The grill was hot and smoking. Dad held up his hand. "Stop there, Athena. Hot things are for grown-ups." Athena stopped. She put her hands behind her back. She watched the smoke curl up. Then she turned around and waved. Dad waved back.

The butterfly flew to the far fence. Athena wanted to follow it. She walked and walked. The tall bushes got in the way. She looked back at the house. She could not see Dad. She could not see the steps. Her tummy felt small and tight. She stood very still and listened. She heard the wind in the leaves. She heard a far-off train. But she could not hear Dad.

Athena called, "Dad!" He called back, "Athena!" His voice came from the steps. She ran toward his voice. The bushes opened up. There was Dad, waving both arms. She ran right into his hug. "I could not see you," she said. "Now you can," said Dad. "Stay where I can see you."

They sat together on the warm steps. Athena counted the butterflies. One, two, three. "That one is neat," said Dad. He pointed to a small blue one. Athena clapped her hands. She stayed close. Dad smiled and drank his tea.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
Lucy wanted to draw the sky. She got her crayon box and sat at the table. She pulled out a blue crayon. "Too dark," said Lucy. "The sky is not that dark."

Her brother Sam came over. "That crayon is not blue," he said. "It looks too dark to be blue."

"Yes, it is blue," said Lucy. She held it up. "Dark blue is still called blue." Sam made a funny face. "Says who?"

So they lined up the blues. Light blue, blue, dark blue. One, two, three. "Look," said Lucy. "All blue. Some are light. Some are dark."

Sam smiled. "Okay. But the snow in my picture is not white. It is very, very light blue."

Lucy laughed. She drew her sky with light blue. Then she gave her doll a deep green dress and yellow shoes.

"Where is the dark blue now?" asked Lucy.

"Here," said Sam. He drew the night.
